title: The Pinecrest Files
subtitle: Sunday 18 September 1977: The Ice Company Night Log, the Cutters' Ground, and the Man Who Cannot Say His Name

setting.name: Camp Pinecrest, the Office and its attic, the Cutters' Ground, the Director's House and the Outlet below the dam, Sunday 18 September 1977
setting.description: The day the party learns the truth. The rain goes on until early afternoon; the Outlet peaks at noon and begins, very slowly, to fall. Everyone has slept badly or not at all. Somewhere on the Neck the man in the mask is resting, and somewhere under the Boathouse floor the thing that wore Gene's face and Santi's is lying in the black water waiting for dusk. The party has a murderer, a monster and a timetable. What it does not have is a reason, and the reason is in the Office attic, in a tin trunk of ice company papers that nobody has opened since 1933, and in the Director's House, and in an old man's shirt pocket.
setting.atmosphere: Paper, dust and grey light. A research day: the smell of old ledgers, mouse droppings in a trunk, a typewriter in an empty office, the hiss of rain on a tin roof, then, in the afternoon, the rain stopping and a terrible stillness coming over the lake. Let the horror here be the past: copperplate handwriting, a blurred face in a 1914 photograph, a gravestone with no name. Then let the present arrive in a rowboat on the flood.

keyLocations.name: The Office
keyLocations.description: The ice company's counting house of 1881, a clapboard building of two rooms and an attic between the Lodge and the dam, now the camp office: Opal's desk, a typewriter, a switchboard that served the one line, wooden filing cabinets with forty-four years of Pinecrest in them, a safe, and a ladder to the attic hatch. The phone on the desk is dead.
features: The filing cabinets: guest registers 1934–1977; staff files; Philomena Delamater's correspondence; the directors' memos
The safe: the camp's cash box ($212), the deeds, and a Smith & Wesson service revolver that has been in it since 1946 (Coach has the combination; so does Opal)
The attic ladder and hatch, padlocked; Opal has the key on her ring
encounters: Opal Seeley, who has not left her desk since seven, typing a list of everyone on the Neck for the State Police
secrets: CLUE C1 (core): in Philomena's correspondence, a printed card, LANTERN NIGHT, 1934, with her handwritten instructions for the staff on the back: 'Masks on before the dock, off after the beach. Lanterns down, eyes up. No one on the water after. — P.D. (Mr. Dreher says the Lake must keep no faces. I have promised him.)'

Herbert Amsel's memo, 10 September 1962, to all staff: 'The so-called Lantern Night masks are morbid and old-fashioned, they frighten the guests, and Life magazine's photographer will not want them. They will not be used this year. N.A.' Pinned to it, a handwritten note in pencil: 'Mr. Amsel. Please. My father's rule. — A. Dreher.'

Curtis Seeley's staff file, 1955–1962: applications, evaluations, and his letters to the director every spring, in square block print, signed 'Curtis Seeley' with a big looping C. The file ends in 1962 with a resignation letter dated 20 September 1962, in copperplate, signed 'C. Seeley' in a hand nothing like the others (CLUE D4).
The 1965 deed of sale, Pinecrest to Curtis A. Seeley, signed in the same copperplate.

keyLocations.name: The Ice Company Attic
keyLocations.description: A low, dusty attic under the Office roof, lit by one small window at each gable end: broken chairs, Pinecrest's old canvas tents, a dressmaker's dummy, and in the corner under a tarpaulin a black tin trunk stencilled LANTERN LAKE ICE CO. — RECORDS, padlocked with a rusted lock that opens to a crowbar in one pull.
features: The night log, 1884 to 1932: eleven ruled ledgers in canvas covers, one line for every night gang that went out on the ice, kept by the superintendent
The payroll books, 1881 to 1932, with each man's signature or mark beside his wages
A cardboard box of photographs: the ice gangs on the lake, every winter from 1890 to 1931, men in caps and mufflers with saws and hooks and horses
A tide of mouse-shredded paper and sawdust
encounters: Nobody. The rain on the roof is very loud.
secrets: The night log, January 1888, in a superintendent's hand: 'Jan. 19. Night gang on No. 3 channel. A man come up out of the cut with young Ehrhardt's face and would not say his name. G. Brodt the foreman knew it for Mathias Kintner who was lost in the cut last winter by the way it stood, and called it so, Mathias Kintner, to its face, and it went down. Ehrhardt unhurt. G.B. says the old men knew it so. Let it be wrote.' (CLUE C5, core.)
December 1913: 'Dec. 11. The man Smith of No. 2 gang went through at the foot of No. 4 at 2 in the morning and was not found. No man knows his true name or his people. B.V.' (Rudolph Dreher.)

January 1914, in Rudolph's hand, the core of it: 'Jan. 22. Night gang No. 2, No. 4 channel. L. Garside saw his face on the water by lantern and it did not move with him, so he says. Jan. 23. Garside is not right. Will not say his name, will not look in the glass in the bunkhouse. Jan. 23 night. Two of Garside seen, one on the ice and one in the bunkhouse. Jan. 24. Garside rode out on the morning ice train over the Outlet trestle and has not come back. God forgive me I put him on it. Jan. 25. Hoods for all night gangs henceforth. No man to look on open water by lantern unhooded. No man to ride out the morning after he is seen twice. If ever it come again, call it by its name, as Brodt done.' (CLUE C1, C2, C3, C4, C5.)

The 1913 payroll: LORENZ GARSIDE, $1.75 a day, signed in a beautiful, careful copperplate, every week, the same hand that signed Curtis Seeley's 1962 resignation and the 1965 deed (CLUE D4, the truth of it, DC 20, for anyone who lays them side by side). The 1914 payroll, after 24 January: no Garside.

The ice gang photographs: winter 1913, No. 2 gang on the ice, LORENZ GARSIDE in the back row, a lanky young man with a thin moustache, laughing. Winter 1914, February, the same gang, and in the back row, labelled L. GARSIDE (visiting), a figure whose face is a soft grey smear, exactly like Coach's in the staff photographs. The thing that rode out as Lorenz in 1914 came back to visit the gang once. (The truth of it, DC 20.)

keyLocations.name: The Cutters' Ground
keyLocations.description: A burying ground on the knoll above the dam, half an acre of laurel and hemlock inside a low iron fence with a gate, with forty-odd stones: ice company men from 1884 to 1951, most of them small grey slabs with a name, two dates and sometimes a line. From the knoll you can see the whole lake, the dam and the flooded Outlet.
features: RUDOLPH DREHER — 1880–1946 — SUPT. LANTERN LAKE ICE CO. — HE KEPT THE NIGHT GANGS
GOTTLOB BRODT — 1841–1909 — FOREMAN
LORENZ GARSIDE — 1886–1951 — a plain stone, no line
A small stone with no name: A MAN OF THE ICE GANG — LOST UNDER THE ICE DEC. 11 1913 — HIS NAME IS KNOWN TO GOD
MATHIAS KINTNER — 1848–1887 — LOST UNDER THE ICE — FOUND AND LAID 1888
encounters: Alvin Dreher, by his father's grave at noon, if he has not been caught
secrets: MATHIAS KINTNER's stone (Investigation DC 10 to read it rightly): FOUND AND LAID, in 1888, a year after he was lost. He was never found in the lake; he was 'laid' when Brodt called him by name. Somebody carved that on purpose. (CLUE C5.)

LORENZ GARSIDE 1886–1951 is a red herring as well as a clue: the man under it lived Lorenz's life from 1914 to 1951 and was the nameless 'Smith' of December 1913. Lorenz Garside himself was in the lake from 1914 until 1962. Saying 'Lorenz Garside' to Old Glass now does nothing.

The nameless stone: the reason a nameless drowned man was a danger. Occult DC 14, or Zachary's Old Lore: a soul the lake keeps with no name to be called by cannot be laid by calling. That is why Smith's Old Glass could never have been laid, and why it took a life instead. The one in the lake now has a name.

keyLocations.name: The Director's House
keyLocations.description: A big log house of 1938 on the point at the north end of the Neck, with a stone chimney, a porch on three sides and a view down the whole lake. Coach has lived here since 1965. The door is not locked; nothing on the Neck is.
features: No mirrors anywhere: pale rectangles on the walls where they hung, and a medicine cabinet in the bathroom with its mirror door removed and the hinges bare
Every window facing the lake painted over on the inside, cream, years ago; the windows facing the woods are clear
Coach's desk: account books, bills, Ridgeview correspondence, a letter-opener, and in the drawer a small cardboard box from a Stroudsburg auto parts store
A shelf of books, almost all of them published before 1914: farm almanacs, a hymnal, a cutters' songbook, a primer
A shaving brush and a straight razor by the bathroom sink, and no mirror
encounters: Nobody, if Coach is at the Lodge; Coach himself, if the party comes after 3 p.m. and he is back from the Outlet
secrets: CLUE E2 (core): the box in the desk drawer holds a new distributor rotor and cap for a 1969 Chevrolet, and a receipt dated Tuesday 13 September 1977, three days before Lantern Night. He bought it before anything happened, because he knew Alvin would pull the others.
CLUE D3 (core): no mirrors, and the lakeside windows painted out. A man who will not see his reflection, or will not be seen from the lake. Combined with the photo wall, Rule Two.

Under the songbook on the shelf, a pocket watch, silver, very worn, engraved on the back L.G. 1907. It still runs. It was in the pocket of the coat that rode out on the ice train in 1914, and Lorenz Garside, coming up out of the lake in Curtis's face in 1962, found it that autumn in a junk shop in Larkin Corners, in a box of the things of the man who had lived as Lorenz until 1951, and bought it back for a dollar.
In a drawer of the bedside table, a dozen letters from Opal, 1963 to 1964, unanswered, all beginning 'Dear Curtis'.

keyLocations.name: The Outlet Below the Dam
keyLocations.description: Below the spillway the Outlet runs through a deep pool before it narrows and goes roaring under the flooded bridge. On the far side of the pool a fisherman's path climbs to the road beyond the washout. Normally you could row across the pool in a minute. On Sunday it is a brown whirlpool full of branches.
features: The ice company's flat-bottomed workboat, hauled down from the Boathouse to the pool's edge on rollers
A rope already fixed to a hemlock on this bank, run out across the pool to a snag on the far side
The roar of the spillway, which makes it impossible to hear anyone more than twenty feet away
encounters: Coach and 'Santi' in the workboat at 3 p.m. (Act 3)
secrets: Rowing or hauling the workboat across on the rope: Athletics DC 16 each round for three rounds; two failures and it swamps and turns back. Anyone who crosses the pool in the boat crosses running water, and anything carried in it is carried (Rule Three).

synopsis: On Sunday the rain falls until two and the flood peaks at noon. The party, exhausted, finds the reasons behind everything. In the Office, Philomena Delamater's 1934 instructions ('the Lake must keep no faces'), Herbert Amsel's 1962 memo banning the masks, and Curtis Seeley's staff file, his square print giving way in September 1962 to a copperplate hand. In the attic, the Lantern Lake Ice Company's night log: Mathias Kintner laid by his name in 1888; a nameless cutter lost under the ice in 1913; and in January 1914, 'L. Garside will not say his name ... rode out on the morning ice train ... if ever it come again, call it by its name.' The 1913 payroll shows Lorenz Garside's signature in the same copperplate as Coach's. In the Cutters' Ground, a grave with no name and a stone that reads FOUND AND LAID. Alvin Dreher, found or talked down, tells them the rest: the ride he gave 'Curtis' over the bridge in 1962, the empty canoe, the twelve-year truce, the masks, and what Coach is. In the Director's House, no mirrors, painted windows, Lorenz Garside's 1907 pocket watch, and a rotor bought three days before Lantern Night. At three in the afternoon, Coach and a soaked, silent 'Santi' try to haul the ice company's workboat across the flooded pool below the dam. And at dusk, Coach takes the real Santi down to the dock with a lantern to 'check the boats'.
hook: Sunday 18 September, seven in the morning. Grey light, rain, nobody has slept. Opal is already at her desk in the Office, typing a list of names for the State Police with two fingers, and when the party comes in she looks up and says, without preamble, "I want to show you something of my brother's. I should have shown somebody fifteen years ago."

conclusions.conclusion: Coach is not Curtis Seeley: he is Lorenz Garside, the ice cutter of 1914
clues: D4: the copperplate on the 1913 payroll, the 1962 resignation and the 1965 deed
D3: no mirrors, painted windows, the 1914 photograph with the blurred face
F3: Opal: 'Curtis could swim the lake end to end. Coach can't swim a stroke.'
The 1907 pocket watch engraved L.G. in his house

conclusions.conclusion: The thing in the lake is Curtis Seeley, and it can be laid by his name
clues: C5: the 1888 log entry and the stone, FOUND AND LAID: Brodt called Mathias Kintner by his name
C5: the 1914 log, 'if ever it come again, call it by its name'
F1: the chain: Kintner, the nameless Smith, Garside, and Curtis's empty canoe in 1962
F2: The Thin Place or Old Lore at the dock: it wants its own face, and a name it cannot reach
Philomena's letter to Winnie (Winnie's Persuasion, below)

conclusions.conclusion: Coach raised it on purpose and means to carry it over the Outlet with someone else's face
clues: E2: the rotor bought three days before Lantern Night
E3: the workboat on the flooded pool with 'Santi' in it
E1 (from Friday): the masks put away and Gene asked to look
C4: the 1914 log, 'rode out on the morning ice train over the Outlet trestle'

acts.title: Sunday Morning: The Files
acts.description: From seven to noon: the Office, the attic and Opal. The purpose of this act is the research payoff the investigation has been building to: the masks' real reason, the ice company's rules, and the first proof that Coach is not who he says he is. Every core clue here is automatic for anyone who looks in the right place; rolls give detail and speed.
objectives: Read Philomena's instructions and Amsel's memo
Compare Curtis Seeley's handwriting before and after 1962
Open the ice company trunk and read the night log

scenes.name: Forty-Four Years in a Filing Cabinet
scenes.description: Opal unlocks the cabinets and lets them look at anything. The 1934 Lantern Night card with Philomena's instructions on the back. Amsel's memo of 10 September 1962 with Alvin's pencilled plea pinned to it. Curtis Seeley's staff file: seven years of square block print, cheerful, misspelled, signed with a big looping C; and then, dated 20 September 1962, a resignation letter in exquisite copperplate, signed 'C. Seeley', thanking Mr. Amsel 'for his many kindnesses'. Laid beside it, the 1965 deed of purchase: the same copperplate. Opal watches them see it. (CLUE C1, D4.)
scenes.readAloud: The staff file is a brown accordion folder held with a rubber band that breaks when you touch it. Seven summers of Curtis Seeley, waterfront: applications, schedules, a note to the director in fat block capitals, cheerful and badly spelled, asking for a second lifeguard, signed with a C as big as a fish hook. Then a letter dated 20 September 1962, on Pinecrest paper, in handwriting like an old wedding invitation, every letter joined and shaded and perfect: 'Dear Mr. Amsel, I beg to tender my resignation as of this date, and thank you for your many kindnesses. Respectfully, C. Seeley.' You look from one to the other. They are not the same hand. They are not the same century.

skillChecks.success: Two different writers, without any doubt. The copperplate is a schoolroom hand of the 1890s or 1900s, practised by a man who was taught it young and never learned anything else: the pressure, the slant and the joins are all the same in 1962 and 1965, and they are not a skill you pick up in your thirties. Whoever wrote the resignation learned to write before the First War.
skillChecks.failure: People's handwriting changes. Curtis was upset that week, by all accounts.

skillChecks.success: The guest registers from 1962 show the closing weekend: Lantern Night on Friday 14 September, everyone out on Monday 17th. Curtis Seeley is listed as staff; a note in the margin on Saturday 15th, in Opal's hand, reads 'C.'s canoe found adrift, noon. C. safe in Larkin, A.V. drove him.' And from that Saturday on, every one of the director's daily notes refers to Curtis only as 'C.S.'
skillChecks.failure: Forty-four years of guest registers. You could read for a week.

scenes.name: The Tin Trunk
scenes.description: The attic: dust, the rain loud on the roof, the black trunk stencilled LANTERN LAKE ICE CO. — RECORDS. Zachary, if he is played, has been waiting all weekend for this; Opal has the key to the hatch, and a crowbar does the trunk. The night log is eleven ledgers. Let the players read the key entries in Rudolph Dreher's hand as written in keyLocations (1888, December 1913, January 1914): they are the rules of Old Glass, the 1914 precedent for Coach, and the 1888 precedent for laying it, all in one place. The payroll books and the photographs are underneath. Laid side by side, the 1913 payroll signature LORENZ GARSIDE and the 1962 resignation are the same hand (the truth of it, DC 20). The February 1914 gang photograph shows 'L. GARSIDE (visiting)' with a grey smear for a face (the truth of it, DC 20; one Dread at most for both, as one horror). (CLUE C1–C5, D4, F1.) This is the campaign's key clue (controlFile.theKeyClue).
scenes.readAloud: The night log is ruled ledgers in canvas covers, a line a night, forty-eight winters of them: the gang, the channel, the depth of the ice, the weather, the number of blocks, in brown ink in a careful superintendent's hand. Most of it is weather and arithmetic. Then, in January 1914, the lines get longer. 'Jan. 23. Garside is not right. Will not say his name, will not look in the glass in the bunkhouse.' 'Jan. 23 night. Two of Garside seen, one on the ice and one in the bunkhouse.' 'Jan. 24. Garside rode out on the morning ice train over the Outlet trestle and has not come back. God forgive me I put him on it.' And at the bottom of the page, pressed so hard the nib has torn the paper: 'If ever it come again, call it by its name, as Brodt done.'

skillChecks.success: Following the log back from 1914 finds January 1888: young Ehrhardt's face on a thing from the cut that would not say its name, and Gottlob Brodt calling it 'Mathias Kintner', a man lost the winter before, 'and it went down'. And forward from 1914: twenty years of the same line every winter, HOODS, in the night gangs' column. They kept the rule until the ice company died. (Rule Five, Rule One.)
skillChecks.failure: The log is long and the hand is hard. You find 1914. There is more, but it will take hours.

skillChecks.success: Put together, it is a chain. Kintner was lost under the ice and came back as the thing, and was called by his name and laid. Then a nameless man was lost in 1913 and came back as the thing, and since he had no name to be called by, he could only take a life: Lorenz Garside's. Then Lorenz was the thing in the lake, until 1962, when Curtis Seeley's canoe was found empty. Every one of them was a person. Every one of them could be laid by the right name, if somebody knew it. (F1; with Old Lore, Rule Four and Rule Five.)
skillChecks.failure: It is a set of terrible entries in an old man's hand. What they mean together is not yet clear.

scenes.name: Opal's Brother
scenes.description: Opal, in the Office, at her desk, with the door shut. She has kept a shoebox of Curtis's letters: from Korea in 1952 and 1953, in square print, funny, signed 'Curtis' with the big C; postcards from Florida; birthday cards. And she tells it, at last, once, flatly. Curtis was the best swimmer at Pinecrest; he swam the lake end to end every Labor Day. Their mother died in April 1962. The Monday after Lantern Night 1962 her brother came back from Larkin Corners and he was kind and quiet and polite and he called her 'Opal, dear' and had never once in his life called her 'dear'. He could not swim. He said his shoulder. He would not say his name, ever again, not on the telephone, not on a form; he made everyone call him Coach. He signed 'C.S.' He took down every mirror. She wrote to him for two years and he never answered, and then in 1965 he bought the camp with his half of their mother's money and asked her to keep the books, and she said yes, because if she did not stay she would never find out. "I told myself it was grief. Mother, and the war catching up. Everyone said so. Fifteen years. I have never once heard him say Curtis." (CLUE F3, D1.)
scenes.readAloud: Opal takes off her reading glasses and lets them hang on their chain, and folds her hands on a shoebox. "Curtis could swim this lake end to end. Every Labor Day, from the dock to the north shore and back, and the whole camp out cheering. The Monday after Lantern Night 1962 he came back from Larkin Corners in Alvin's truck, and he called me 'Opal, dear'. He had never called me 'dear' in his life. He was so polite. He couldn't swim a stroke. He said it was his shoulder." She opens the shoebox. Letters, in fat square capitals. "I have never heard him say Curtis. Not once in fifteen years. Not on the telephone. Not to the bank. I told myself it was grief." She looks at you. "I'm a bookkeeper. I know when the numbers don't add up. I've known since the Monday. I just didn't know what they added up to."

skillChecks.success: She has known, in the way you know a thing you will not let yourself think, for fifteen years, and she has stayed beside the man who is not her brother all that time because leaving would mean giving up on Curtis. If anyone can call the thing in the lake by its name, it is Opal. She does not know that yet.
skillChecks.failure: She is grieving, and very angry, and very tired.

skillChecks.success: Winnie, brought in or asked separately, remembers the rest: in 1958 Philomena, dying, wrote Winnie a letter, which Winnie still has in her purse. 'If they ever leave off the masks, and you ever see a face on the water that you know, Winnie, call it by its name, poor soul. That is all it wants. Rudolph told me so.' Winnie thought it was the morphine. (CLUE C5.)
skillChecks.failure: Winnie says Miss Delamater said a lot of things at the end, and goes back to the kitchen.

encounters: None hostile. If anyone watches the Lodge windows this morning from the Office, they see Coach standing at the Lodge porch rail looking at the Office, for a long time, then going back inside.

acts.title: Sunday Midday: The Men Who Knew
acts.description: From noon to three: the Cutters' Ground and Alvin, and the Director's House. The purpose of this act is to turn Alvin from monster to witness, and to give the party proof in Coach's own house. If Alvin was caught on Saturday night, he tells his story in the Lodge instead, away from the windows.
objectives: Find Alvin Dreher at his father's grave, and talk him down
Hear Alvin's account of 1962 and the truce
Read the stones in the Cutters' Ground

scenes.name: The Iron Fence
scenes.description: At noon the rain slackens. On the knoll above the dam, inside the low iron fence of the Cutters' Ground, Alvin Dreher is sitting on the wet grass by his father's stone in Philomena's mask, the ice pike across his knees, looking down at the flooded bridge. He has not slept. If the party comes with Winnie or Opal, he lets them come to the gate. If they come with guns out and no Winnie, he stands, holds up the hand mirror, and goes into the hemlocks. Talking him down is the Masked Killer's 'A Person' (campaignRules, The Man in the Mask): Winnie or Opal, Persuasion DC 13 with proof that they know what he knows (the night log, the photographs, the copperplate), or DC 10 if they say his name and his father's. If it works, he lays the pike on his father's grave and takes the mask off, here, inside the iron fence, away from the water, and he is an exhausted old man with a grey stubble and red eyes, and he says: "I killed that fellow. Marcotte. I want you to know I know it." (The stones: keyLocations.)
scenes.readAloud: Inside the iron fence, among the little grey stones, a big man in a dark wool mackinaw is sitting on the wet grass beside one of them, very still, with a long iron-tipped pike laid across his knees. His face is white and smooth and smiling very slightly, with a gold lantern on its brow, and it is turned toward the bridge, where the brown water is still pouring over the rails. When you come up the path he turns his head. He does not get up. Rain runs down the carved cheeks like tears that have nowhere to go. On the stone beside him: RUDOLPH DREHER, 1880–1946. HE KEPT THE NIGHT GANGS.

skillChecks.success: He lays the pike down along his father's grave and reaches up with both hands and lifts the mask off, and under it is only Alvin: grey stubble, red eyes, a face that has been crying for a day and a half. 'I killed that fellow,' he says. 'Marcotte. There were two of him on the dock and I hit the wrong one. I want you to know I know it.' And then he tells you everything.
skillChecks.failure: He stands up, slowly, and holds the little mirror out toward you at arm's length, and looks at it, and lowers it. 'Not you, then,' he says from behind the mask, the first words you have heard from him. 'Not yet.' And he goes into the trees.

skillChecks.success: Reading the stones: MATHIAS KINTNER, LOST UNDER THE ICE, FOUND AND LAID 1888. A man who was never found, but laid. A NAMELESS stone for December 1913. LORENZ GARSIDE 1886–1951, no line at all. Three of them in a row, as if somebody had wanted them near each other.
skillChecks.failure: Forty-odd ice company men under the laurels. The rain has made the old stones hard to read.

scenes.name: Alvin's Account
scenes.description: Wherever he talks, he wants to be away from the lake and the windows: the Icehouse, the Office, the Lodge kitchen with the curtains drawn. He takes his father's notebook out of his shirt pocket, a cloth-covered book of rules written down in 1914 to 1946 ('As the old men said it to Brodt, and Brodt to me'), and lays it on the table. Then: 1962, Lantern Night without masks; Curtis at the end of the dock looking down a long time; midnight, Curtis's last paddle; seven in the morning, 'Curtis' at the cottage door asking for a lift into Larkin Corners, 'and I drove him. Over the bridge. I didn't know till I came back and they'd found the canoe.' What Coach is: 'He's Garside. Lorenz Garside, that my father put on the ice train in 1914. Fifty years in the lake and he came out in Curtis.' The truce: 'He bought the place in '65 and kept me on. I kept the masks and he let me, and the lake kept quiet, and we never said a word about it, twelve years.' This weekend: 'He put the masks away. He give that fellow the lantern. He wants it to take somebody and go, so it'll quit looking for him.' And why he did what he did: 'Nothing goes over that bridge. Not while I'm alive.' He does not know Rule Five; his father's notebook says 'call it by its name, as Brodt done', and Alvin has always thought it meant Garside, and Garside is up at the Director's House, and the thing in the lake is something he can only hit. If the party has the 1888 entry and puts it together for him, that it is Curtis in the lake, he sits down very hard. (CLUE D6, C1–C4.)
scenes.readAloud: He lays a cloth-covered notebook on the table, soft with handling, and puts his big scarred hand flat on it. "My father wrote this. What the old men told Brodt, and Brodt told him." He does not open it. "Nineteen sixty-two. Seven in the morning, the Saturday. Curtis come to my door, wet, and asked me for a lift into Larkin. Polite. Called me Mister Dreher. Curtis never called me nothing but Al in his life." His hand closes on the book. "And I drove him. Over the bridge. I didn't know. I come back and they'd found his canoe out on the lake, empty, and I knew." He looks up at you. "That's Lorenz Garside up there in the Director's House. My father put him on the ice train in 1914. Fifty years in the lake, and he come up out of it wearing Curtis. And this weekend he put the masks away. He wants it to take somebody else and go." He takes a long breath. "Nothing goes over that bridge. Not while I'm alive."

skillChecks.success: Every word of it is true, and he has never said any of it aloud before. He is not ill and he is not raving; he is a careful man who has believed something terrible on good evidence for fifteen years, and has just found out what it costs to be right about it in the dark.
skillChecks.failure: He believes it absolutely. You don't know yet what you believe.

skillChecks.success: His father's notebook says the rules exactly as the log does, and adds one: 'It cannot cross the Outlet but carried. It sleeps under the boat house.' And at the end, underlined: 'Call it by its name, as Brodt done.' Alvin has always thought that meant Garside's name. It doesn't. It means the name of whoever is in the lake now. (Rule Five; Alvin does not know it until the party tells him.)
skillChecks.failure: A notebook of an old man's rules. You will need time with it.

scenes.name: A House With No Mirrors
scenes.description: The Director's House, while Coach is at the Lodge or out at the Outlet. No mirrors anywhere, pale rectangles where they hung, the medicine cabinet's mirror door off its hinges. The lakeside windows painted cream from the inside, years ago; the woodside windows clear. A straight razor and a brush by a sink with no glass over it. A shelf of pre-1914 books: almanacs, a primer, a cutters' songbook. Under the songbook, a silver pocket watch engraved L.G. 1907, still running. In the desk, the parts-store box: a rotor and cap for a 1969 Chevrolet, and the receipt, dated Tuesday 13 September 1977. In the bedside table, Opal's unanswered letters, 'Dear Curtis'. (CLUE D3, E2.) If Coach comes home and finds them here, he does not shout. He sits down in his chair with his back to the painted windows and says, "Well, friends." (Act 3, Confronting Coach.)
scenes.readAloud: It is a fine, big, comfortable log house, and it takes you a minute to understand what is wrong with it. There are no mirrors. None. Pale rectangles on the pine walls where they used to hang. The bathroom medicine cabinet has no door, only two bare brass hinges. A straight razor and a badger brush lie by the sink, and there is nothing over the sink to shave in. And every window on the lake side of the house, every one, has been painted over from the inside, cream, years ago, so that the room is lit only from the woods behind. Whoever lives here does not look at himself. Or does not want to be looked at, from the water.

skillChecks.success: In the desk drawer, a small box from a Stroudsburg auto parts store: a new rotor and cap for a 1969 Chevrolet. The receipt is dated Tuesday 13 September 1977. Three days before Lantern Night. Three days before anyone pulled a rotor from anything. He knew. (CLUE E2.)
skillChecks.failure: Bills, accounts, Ridgeview letters. A tidy desk.

skillChecks.success: Under a cutters' songbook on the shelf, a silver pocket watch, very worn, still ticking. On the back, engraved in a jeweller's flourish: L.G. 1907.
skillChecks.failure: A shelf of old books, almanacs and a hymnal. He likes old things.

encounters: Alvin Dreher (Masked Killer) if the talk goes badly: he will not fight Winnie or Opal, and retreats from everyone else. If the party attacks him at the Cutters' Ground, he fights to get out of the fence and away; he will not die there if he can help it, because the water is going down.

acts.title: Sunday Afternoon and Dusk: The Boat on the Outlet
acts.description: From three to dusk at 7:40: the boat, the confrontation, and the lake seeing Santi. The purpose of this act is to show Coach acting, to give the players the chance to face him, and to set up the last night. If the party put Old Glass down on Saturday night, it has no face by day and Coach is at the pool alone, readying the workboat on the rope for Monday; play the scene as a rehearsal and a confrontation.
objectives: Stop the boat on the flooded Outlet
Go to the dock at dusk and learn what the thing wants
Notice that Coach has taken Santi to the dock

scenes.name: The Workboat
scenes.description: At three the rain stops. From the dam or the Cutters' Ground, someone sees two figures at the pool below the spillway hauling the ice company's flat workboat into the brown water along a fixed rope: Coach, in his yellow slicker, and Santi Rivera, soaked to the skin, bareheaded, silent. The real Santi is wherever the party left him. Fear check, seeing it, DC 15. Coach is trying to carry 'Santi' over running water before dusk (Rule Four: worn Saturday night, it must be carried before Sunday dusk). The pool is a whirlpool; they get a third of the way and swamp (Athletics DC 16, two failures; or the party gets there first). The party can cut the rope, haul the boat back, or call out. If anyone says 'Santi' to the thing in the boat, it does nothing; if the real Santi is brought and looks it in the eyes and says 'I'm Santiago Rivera', it runs out of his clothes into the bottom of the boat as lake water (Rule Four; it can never wear his face again; Coach's plan needs a new face). If Alvin sees the boat, he comes down the dam at a run with the pike, and Coach shoots at him with the office revolver.
scenes.readAloud: The rain has stopped. In the sudden quiet the roar of the spillway is enormous. Below the dam, in the brown whirling pool, the old flat-bottomed ice boat is out on the water, a third of the way across, hauled along a rope hand over hand. In the stern, in a yellow slicker, the big man you all call Coach, pulling for his life. In the bow, sitting very upright, soaking wet and bareheaded and perfectly still, his hands folded in his lap: Santi Rivera. You left Santi in the Lodge half an hour ago. As you watch, the Santi in the boat turns his head and looks up at you on the dam, and smiles, a little uncertainly, the way Santi does.

skillChecks.success: You get down the bank to the rope's anchor before the boat is halfway, and you can cut it, or haul on it, or simply hold it. The boat swings broadside in the current, ships a sheet of brown water and comes round. Coach stares at you over the gunwale with an expression you will not forget. Not anger. Despair.
skillChecks.failure: The bank is mud and laurel and you slide most of it. By the time you reach the rope the boat has swamped on its own, turned back by the current, and Coach is hauling it in to the near bank, soaked, and the thing in the bow is gone over the side into the pool without a sound.

skillChecks.success: Coach is not trying to escape. He is trying to deliver something across the water before the light goes. He keeps looking at the sky.
skillChecks.failure: He is in a boat on a flood with a thing in Santi's face. That is all you need to know.

scenes.name: Confronting Coach
scenes.description: Wherever it happens (the pool bank, the Director's House, the Lodge), Coach does not run and does not shout. Faced with the copperplate, the watch, the receipt, the log, he sits down with his back to the nearest window and says, "Well, friends." What he says next depends on how he is approached. Treated as a murderer, he says he has killed no one, which is true. Treated as a monster, he says nothing. Treated as a man (by Opal, by Winnie, by anyone who says 'Lorenz'), he tells some of it: "You don't know what it is down there. Forty-eight years. No face. No name. Cold. You forget your mother. You forget your hands. And then a face, and you come up into it, and it's morning, and you're warm." He will not say 'Curtis'. He cannot. Asked to say his own name, 'Lorenz Garside', he goes grey and says he cannot do that either, and that is not true: he can, and it is the one thing that would save him if the thing ever wears his face (Rule Four), and it is the one thing he is most afraid of in the world, because then Opal will have heard it. He asks them, very simply, to let him go on Monday. If held, he goes quietly; if left free, he goes back to his plan (pc-scenario-004). Nolan can arrest him for nothing that will stand up in Stroudsburg.
scenes.readAloud: He sits down slowly in the nearest chair with his back to the window, and puts his big calloused hands on his knees, and looks at the watch, or the receipt, or the photograph, for a long time. "Well, friends," he says. When he speaks again his voice is different: lower, slower, with an accent you have never heard in it, Pennsylvania mountain, old. "You don't know what it is down there. Forty-eight years. No face. No name. Cold. You forget your mother. You forget you had hands. And then one night there's a face on the water and a light, and you come up into it, and it's morning, and you're warm." He looks at you, and his eyes are wet. "I didn't ask for it. Neither did he. I only want to go."

skillChecks.success: Opal, or whoever has reached him: he admits the masks, the lantern, Gene, the rotor and the boat. He admits that the thing in the lake is Curtis, and that it has been looking at him out of every dark window for fifteen years. 'It wants its face, see. My face. His face.' He will not say his own name. Not yet.
skillChecks.failure: He says he has done nothing a court would call a crime, and that they should ask Alvin about Marcotte, and goes very quiet.

skillChecks.success: He is terrified of two things. One is the lake. The other is Opal hearing him say 'Lorenz Garside' out loud, because then fifteen years of being her brother's kindly ghost are over and he is only a stranger who stole her brother's life. He would almost rather go back in the water.
skillChecks.failure: An old man in a younger man's body, frightened and stubborn.

scenes.name: Dusk at the Dock
scenes.description: At about 7:30 the sky clears in the west for the first time in two days and the lake goes absolutely still, a black mirror under a green sky. A Sensitive using The Thin Place on the dock, or an Occultist's Old Lore, or anyone who sits at the end of the dock and listens, can learn what it wants (CLUE F2): a longing like someone at a window, for a face, a particular face, its own, and under it a name it reaches for and cannot reach, as on the tip of the tongue; and a song, a slow waltz. If Marvin plays the 1958 'Lantern Lake Waltz' at the Lodge piano with the doors open, something stands up in the water off the end of the dock, faceless, and listens. Meanwhile, unless the party has him, Coach has gone to Santi (or his new choice) and asked him to help 'check the boats' at the Boathouse before dark, with a lantern; and at dusk Santi stands on the Boathouse float with a lantern while Coach fusses with a mooring, and looks down at the still water. Then Coach says, 'Alvin's out there, pal. I've got a safe place for you,' and walks him to the Icehouse, and locks the door. End the scenario with the sun going, someone counting heads in the Lodge, and Santi not there.
scenes.readAloud: The sky has cleared in the west for the first time in two days and the lake has gone still, perfectly still, a sheet of black glass under a sky the colour of a bottle. Every hemlock on the far shore stands upside down in it. There is no sound at all but the spillway, far off. You sit on the end of the dock with your feet over the water and open yourself to the place, and it comes up through the planks like cold through a floor: someone waiting. Someone at a window in the dark, looking out at a lit house where they used to live, waiting for someone to say a word. A name. Their name. It is right there. They cannot reach it. And from very far down, from the bottom of the lake, faint and slow, three-four time, a waltz.

skillChecks.success: It wants its own face back, and its own name, and it cannot find either. It will take any face to get out, but it would rather have its own. And it cannot say its name, because it no longer remembers it. Somebody has to say it for it. (CLUE F2; Rule Five.)
skillChecks.failure: Cold, and longing, and a waltz. You do not know what to do with any of it.

skillChecks.success: From the dock, you can see the Boathouse float. Santi is standing on it with a lantern held out over the water, looking down, and Coach is beside him, not looking, his face turned away toward the shore. Then Coach puts a hand on his shoulder, and they walk up the path toward the dam, toward the Icehouse.
skillChecks.failure: The lake, the sky, the last of the light. It is very beautiful. It is very quiet.

encounters: Old Glass (The Fetch) in the workboat in Santi's face, if it was not put down on Saturday night; it fights only to stay in the boat or reach the water
Coach (Night Watchman) with the office revolver: he shoots only at Alvin, and misses on purpose if anyone else is in the way
Alvin Dreher (Masked Killer), if he sees the boat: he comes for it and for Coach

npcsInvolved.name: 'Coach' Seeley, 45 (Lorenz Garside, born 1886)
npcsInvolved.role: Director; the one who raised it
npcsInvolved.description: Calm all morning; at the Outlet with the workboat at three; in his chair with his back to the window when confronted, speaking at last in an old mountain voice.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To carry the thing over the water before dusk in Santi's face, or failing that, before Monday's dawn.

npcsInvolved.name: Alvin Dreher, 58
npcsInvolved.role: The man in the mask, at his father's grave; the witness
npcsInvolved.description: Exhausted, red-eyed, his father's notebook in his shirt pocket; takes the mask off inside the iron fence.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be believed, to be stopped, and to keep anything from crossing the bridge.

npcsInvolved.name: Opal Seeley, 41
npcsInvolved.description: A shoebox of letters in square print, and fifteen years of not saying it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To know, at last. And, once she knows, to get her brother out of the lake.

npcsInvolved.name: Winifred "Winnie" Szot, 63
npcsInvolved.description: Philomena's 1958 letter in her purse; the one person Alvin will always listen to.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To bring Alvin in alive, and to do what Miss Delamater asked her twenty years ago.

npcsInvolved.name: Santiago "Santi" Rivera, 25
npcsInvolved.role: The rodman whose face it is wearing (a companion)
npcsInvolved.description: Frightened, angry and very brave; the person the thing in the boat looks like.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get his face back, if that is what it takes.

npcsInvolved.name: Marvin Eckhart, 64
npcsInvolved.description: Knows every revue song, including the 1958 Lantern Lake Waltz, which Curtis used to whistle.
npcsInvolved.motivation: If somebody tells him a song will help, he will play it until his hands bleed.

npcsInvolved.name: Rudolph Dreher (1880–1946)
npcsInvolved.role: Superintendent of the Lantern Lake Ice Company; author of the night log
npcsInvolved.description: His hand in the log, his rules in the notebook, his stone in the Cutters' Ground: HE KEPT THE NIGHT GANGS.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He put Lorenz Garside on the ice train in 1914, and spent the rest of his life making sure nobody else rode out.

npcsInvolved.name: Philomena Delamater (1889–1959)
npcsInvolved.description: A store's personnel director from Philadelphia who bought a failed ice company for a grown-ups' camp, and kept a promise to its superintendent for twenty-five years.
npcsInvolved.motivation: 'The Lake must keep no faces. I have promised him.'

npcsInvolved.name: Herbert Amsel
npcsInvolved.role: Director of Pinecrest, 1960 to 1964; retired to Florida
npcsInvolved.description: Known only by his 1962 memo banning the masks for the sake of a magazine photographer.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A modern camp for a modern public.

rewards.money: No money changes hands. The camp's cash box holds $212, which Opal will give to Nolan for safekeeping. Coach, if confronted, offers to sign the whole of the Ridgeview purchase money over to Opal on Monday if they let him go; it is $410,000, and he means it.
items: The night log of the Lantern Lake Ice Company, 1884–1932, and the January 1888 and January 1914 entries (CLUE C1–C5)
The 1913 payroll with LORENZ GARSIDE in copperplate, and the 1962 resignation in the same hand (CLUE D4)
Rudolph Dreher's notebook of rules, from Alvin's shirt pocket
Philomena Delamater's 1958 letter to Winnie: 'call it by its name, poor soul'
The auto parts box and receipt dated 13 September 1977 (CLUE E2)
Opal's shoebox of Curtis's letters, which a person who knew him can hold while saying his name

twists: The players will want Lorenz Garside's grave to be the answer: dig it up, burn the bones, say the name on the stone. The grave holds the nameless cutter of 1913, whose name is lost forever, which is why that Old Glass could never be laid. The one in the lake now has a name, and his sister is in the Office.

Coach is not evil in any way he would understand. He spent forty-eight years faceless in a lake because someone else took his life, and when he came up into a warm morning he did exactly what was done to him. He is also, this weekend, prepared to do it to a twenty-five-year-old veteran he has known for two days. Both are true.

Alvin's father's notebook says 'call it by its name, as Brodt done', and Alvin has believed for fifteen years that it meant Garside, who is alive and sitting in the Director's House. The players can give Alvin the answer he never had. Watch what it does to him.

Coach can save himself whenever the thing wears his face, by saying "Lorenz Garside" to it. He knows this. He would rather have someone else go into the lake than say it in front of Opal. That is the whole of him, and the whole of the finale.

If the real Santi names himself to the thing in the boat, Coach needs a new face by Sunday dusk. He will choose the loneliest person left on the Neck, which is often a player character who has spent the weekend alone at a window.
dmTips: This is a research scenario. Make the documents physical: read out the log entries in Rudolph's voice, put the two signatures side by side, let the player hold the 1914 photograph. The horror is in the paper.

Every core clue is automatic for anyone who looks in the right place: the log, the payroll, Philomena's card, the receipt, the house with no mirrors. Rolls add detail and speed. Never let a failed roll hide the 1888 entry or the copperplate.
Talking Alvin down should be Winnie's or Opal's scene, with the players supporting them. Give the NPC the moment; it is earned.
Coach's confession, if it comes, should be quiet and sad, in a voice from 1910. He is the campaign's tragedy. Do not let him become a cackling villain, and do not let him off.
The workboat is the scenario's set piece. Make it physical: the rope, the roar, the brown water, the thing in the bow turning its head to smile at them in Santi's face.

Make sure, by dusk, that the players know or can work out all five of Old Glass's rules and that its name is Curtis Seeley. If they are missing Rule Five, let Winnie remember Philomena's letter, or let The Thin Place give it on the dock.
End on the head count in the Lodge and Santi missing. The last night starts there.
Budget an hour for the Office and the attic, an hour for Alvin and the Director's House, and an hour for the boat, Coach and dusk.
